items.title: Reverse Sequential Proportional Approval Voting Rule: Proportionality and Approximation Guarantees

items.summary: A virtual screen of 1,134 candidate perturbations over a single-cell perturbation-response model returned no improving candidate in any of nine scoring spaces. This report shows that the unanimous negative is arithmetic rather than evidence, and that no candidate could have ranked well for reasons internal to the scoring metric and the model. Two measurements establish this, neither requiring ground truth. First, scoring the library against the starting population instead of the target leaves the ranking essentially unchanged: for the screen's production metric, entropically regularized optimal transport, Spearman rho between the two rankings is +0.976, with 80 of the top 100 candidates shared. A metric whose ranking does not change when the destination changes is measuring effect size and reporting it as efficacy. Second, 90.5 percent of the model's per-cell response variance is a single vector applied to every compound in the library, rising to 97.9 percent of the variance the screen actually scores after its mean-over-cells pooling. That shared vector is nearly perpendicular to the start-to-target direction (cosine +0.063) and longer than the distance to be traveled, and it does not reverse when the task is reversed, so it is a property of the model rather than of the task. The report proposes a two-part precondition on any perturbation-ranking metric. Part one, replicate consistency, is imported unchanged from image-based profiling and asks whether the metric resolves the identity of the perturbing agent. Part two, the self-target control, asks whether the ranking changes when the target is replaced by the starting population. Part two consumes no ground truth, which distinguishes it from the published perturbation-specificity metrics surveyed here, all of which require observed post-perturbation data. A scoring space is exhibited that passes part one at ten standard errors while carrying essentially no directional content, so both parts can pass and the ranking still be worthless. Mode collapse in perturbation-response models is published and is not claimed here. What is reported is how much of one real model's response it accounts for, a task-reversal control establishing that the shared component belongs to the model rather than to the task, and the consequence for the screening setting, which the nearest benchmark considered and explicitly declined to evaluate. The errors made along the way are reported rather than removed. A unanimous negative was drafted as a finding before the control that disqualified it was run, and three further conclusions were each stated after one check and before the check that would have overturned them. All are withdrawn in the text, with the reasoning left visible, because that pattern is the subject of the paper. Analysis code, the notebook, and a notebook-integrity checker are at https://github.com/glenritschel/pharos-direction-control. The query populations derive from GEO accession GSE136103 (Ramachandran et al., Nature 2019). The two cell-state annotations are the author's own and are not part of that deposit, so reproducing the task requires the annotation step and not only the accession.
items.title: A virtual screen that could not have succeeded: scoring metrics that rank by effect size and report it as efficacy

items.summary: Unrefereed candidate: an Eulerian-flow transfer and exact local window U_p intersect [alpha,691/250] = {2}, for every fixed 0<p<1. Full homogeneous finite simple bunkbed counterexamples exist at the other weights in this window. The graph may depend on both parameters. Alpha is not a record lower endpoint. Global classification and integer q>=3 remain unresolved. Producer-side exact reconstruction and negative controls; no formal verification or external human peer review established. Original prose/data CC0-1.0, original code MIT; third-party material retains its terms.
items.title: Flow-polynomial obstructions to the random-cluster bunkbed inequality
